'''yew'''<sup>1</sup> (yö), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''yewe'', ''yeugh'', ''ewe'', ''eugh'', ''ewgh'', ''yowe''; < ME. ''ew'', ''u'', < AS. ''īw'' (in an early gloss. ''iuu''), also ''eów'' = D. ''ijf'' = OHG. ''īwa'', MHG. ''iwe'', G. ''eibe'' = Icel. ''ȳr'', yew (MHG. and Icel. also a bow of yew); also, in another form, AS. ''eóh'' = OLG. ''īch'' = OHG. ''īha'', G. dial. (Swiss) ''iche'', ''ige''; cf. F. ''if'', Sp. ''iva'', ML. ''ivus'', yew (< OHG.); OIr. ''ēo'' (mod. Ir. ''iubhar'', Gael. ''iubhar'', ''iughar'') = W. ''yw'', ''ywen'' = Corn. ''hivin'' = Bret. ''ivin'', ''ivinen'', yew; the Celtic forms being possibly original.]   '''1.''' A tree of the genus ''Taxus'',
the common yew being ''T. baccata'' of temperate Europe and Asia. {{smaller|This is a slow-growing and long-lived evergreen of moderate height and spreading habit, with a thick irregular trunk and dark thick foliage. In Europe the yew has long been planted in graveyards. There are several dwarf, weeping, and variegated varieties. The golden yew has the edge of the leaves in spring of a bright-golden yellow. The Irish yew (var. ''fastigiata'') has erect branches, and is more hardy than the typical form, which will not endure the winter in the northern United States. The wood of the yew is heavy, fine-grained, and elastic, and was formerly much used for bows, the supply being protected by government. It is considered a very choice cabinet-wood, the heart being of a fine orange-red or deep brown, and the sap-wood white. The leaves of the tree are poisonous.}}
{{smaller block|The sheter ''ew'', the asp for shaftes pleyne. {{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 180.}}}}
{{smaller block|The twigs and leaves of ''yew'', though eaten in a very small quantity, are certain death to horses and cows, and that in a few minutes.
{{right|''Gilbert White'', Antiquities of Selborne, v.}}}}
'''2.''' The wood of the yew-tree.
{{smaller block|A bow made of the best foreign ''yew'', six shillings and eightpence. {{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 121.}}}}
'''3.''' A shooting-bow made of the wood of the yew.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tubal (with his ''Yew''
And ready quiver) did a Boar pursue.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Handy-Crafts.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wing’d arrows from the twanging ''yew''.</poem>
{{right|''Gay'', The Fan, i.}}}}

{{c|{{smaller|Yew (''Taxus baccata'').}}}}

{{smaller|'''American yew''', specifically, ''Taxus Canadensis'', or, as often classified, ''T. baccata'', variety ''Canadensis'', a prostrate shrub with straggling branches, common in dark woods; ground-hemlock. There are three other American yews, for which see ''short-leafed yew'' and ''Taxus''.—'''California yew''', the short-leafed yew.—'''Golden yew, Irish yew.''' See def. 1.—'''Japan yew''', a tree of the genus ''Cephalotaxus''. There is also a true yew in Japan. See ''Taxus''.—'''Mexican yew''', ''Taxus globosa''.—'''Short-leafed yew''', ''Taxus brevifolia'', of Pacific North America, a not abundant tree, at its best from 50 to 70 feet high. Its wood is hard, heavy, and very fine-grained, susceptible of a beautiful polish, and very durable in contact with the soil; it is used for fence-posts, and by the Indians for paddles, bows, etc. ''Sargent''.—'''Stinking yew.''' See ''stink''.—'''Western yew''', the short-leafed yew.—'''Yew family''', the suborder ''Taxaceæ'' of the ''Coniferæ''.}}

{{right|''Character of a Fanatic'' (Harl. Misc., VII. 637). (''Nares.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|The juyce of the roots [of skirret] helpeth the hicket, or ''yeoxing.''

{{right|''Abr. Flem. Nomenclator'', 432 b. (''Nares.'')}}}}

Its roots run in three directions: one to the Asa gods in heaven, one to the Frost-giants, and the third to the under-world. Under each root is a fountain of wonderful virtues. In the tree, which drops honey, sit an eagle, a squirrel, and four stags. Also called ''Tree of the Universe.''}}

'''Yid, Yiddisher''' (yid, yid′ish-ėr), ''n.''   [< G. ''jüdisch, jüdischer'', Jewish.]   A Jew. ''Leland.'' [Slang, London.]

'''Yiddish''' (yid′ish), ''a.''   [< G. ''jüdisch'', Jewish.]   Jewish. ''Athenæum'', No. 3303, p. 212. [Slang, London.]

'''yield''' (yēld), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''yeeld''; < ME. ''yelden, ȝelden'' (pret. ''yald, yolde'', pp. ''yolden, ȝolden''), < AS. ''geldan, gildan, gyldan, gieldan'' (pret. ''geald'', pl. ''guldon'', pp. ''golden''), give up, pay, yield, restore, = OS. ''geldan'' = OFries. ''jelda'' = D. ''gelden'' = OHG. ''geltan'', MHG. G. ''gelten'' = Icel. ''gjalda'' = Sw. ''gälla'' = Dan. ''gjelde'', be worth, be of consequence, avail, = Goth. *''gildan'', in comp. ''fragildan'' (= AS. ''forgeldan''), pay back, ''usgildan'' (= AS. ''āgeldan''), pay back. Cf. Lith. ''galeti'', be able, have power; W. ''gallu'', be able. Hence ult. ''gild''<sup>2</sup>, ''guilt''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To give in payment; pay; repay; reward; requite; recompense.
{{smaller block|Lord, what may i for that ''ȝylde'' the?
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 195.}}}}
{{smaller block|God ''yelde'' the, frend. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 1055.}}}}
{{smaller block|Feire lady, with goode will, and gramercy of youre seruyse; and God graunte me power that I may yow this guerdon ''yelde''. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 227.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''King.'' How do you, pretty lady?
''Oph.'' Well, God ’''ild'' you!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 5. 41.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>God ''yield'' ye, and God thank ye!</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, iv. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The good mother holds me still a child!
Good mother is bad mother unto me!
A worse were better; yet no worse would I.
Heaven ''yield'' her for it.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Gareth and Lynette.}}}}
'''2.''' To give in return, or by way of recompense; produce, as a reward or return for labor performed, capital invested, or some similar output.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rememberynge him that love to wyde yblowe
''Yelt'' bitter fruyt, though swete sede be sowe.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 385.}}}}
{{smaller block|When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth ''yield'' unto thee her strength. {{right|Gen. iv. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It was never made, sir,
For threescore pound, I assure you; ’twill ''yield'' thirty.
The plush, sir, cost three pound ten shillings a yard.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Strabo tells us that the Mines at Carthagena ''yielded'' the Romans per diem to the value of twenty-five thousand Drachms. {{right|''Arbuthnot'', Ancient Coins, p. 194.}}}}
{{smaller block|The only fruit which even much living ''yields'' seems to be often only some trivial success.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Letters, p. 19.}}}}
'''3.''' To produce generally; bring forth; give out; emit; bear; furnish.
{{smaller block|Many things doth Asia ''yeeld'' not elsewhere to be had.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 51.}}}}
{{smaller block|No one Clergie in the whole Christian world ''yeelds'' so many eminent schollers, learned preachers, grave, holy, and accomplish’d Divines as this Church of England doth at this day. {{right|''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ammoniated alum ''yields'' a reddish yellow precipitate.
{{right|''Ure'', Dict., III. 365.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Air-swept lindens ''yield''
Their scent. ''M. Arnold'', The Scholar-Gipsy.</poem>}}
'''4.''' To afford; confer; grant; give.

{{smaller block|In hast themperour hendely his gretyng him ''ȝeldes'', and a-non riȝttes after askes his name.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 235.}}}}

{{smaller block|Natheless Poliphemus, wood for his blynde visage, ''yald'' to Ulixes joy by his sorwful teeres.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iv. meter 7.}}}}

<poem>Doubtless Burgundy will ''yield'' him help,
And we shall have more wars before ’t be long.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 6. 90.}}}}

{{smaller block|Where the holy Trinity did first ''yelde'' it-selfe in sensible apparition to the world. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 104.}}}}

<poem>And slowly was my mother brought
To ''yield'' consent to my desire.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Miller’s Daughter.}}}}

'''5.''' To give up, as to a superior power or authority; quit possession of, as through compulsion, necessity, or duty; relinquish; resign; surrender: often followed by ''up''.

<poem>To ''ȝelde'' his loue haue y no myȝte,
But loue him hertili therfore.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|The people were so ouersette with their enemies that manye of them were as ''yolden'', and tooke partie againe their owne neighboures.
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chron. (ed. 1559), I. 62.}}}}

<poem>The fierce lion will hurt no ''yielden'' things.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Wyatt'', To His Lady, Cruel over Her Yielding Lover.}}}}

{{smaller block|Generals of armies, when they have finished their work, are wont to ''yield up'' such commissions as were given them for that purpose. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, viii. 4.}}}}

<poem>My life, I do confess, is hers;
She gives it; and let her take it back; I ''yield'' it.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Sea Voyage, iv. 2.}}}}

'''6.''' To give up or render generally.

{{smaller block|The thef . . . ''ȝelte'' hym creaunt to Cryst on the crosse.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xii. 193.}}}}

{{smaller block|If it is bad to ''yield'' a blind submission to authority, it is not less an error to deny to it its reasonable weight.
{{right|''Gladstone'', Might of Right, p. 245.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Life to ''yield'',
To give it up to heal no city’s shame
In hope of gaining long-enduring fame.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 318.}}}}
'''7.''' To admit the force, justice, or truth of; allow; concede; grant.
{{smaller block|<poem>Pensive I ''yeeld'' I am, and sad in mind,
Through great desire of glory and of fame.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. ix. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis a grievous case this, I do ''yield'', and yet not to be despaired. {{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 651.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''yield'' it just, said Adam, and submit.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 526.}}}}
{{smaller block|This was the fourth man that we lost in this Land-Journey; for those two men that we left the day before did not come to us till we were in the North Seas, so we ''yielded'' them also for lost. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 17.}}}}

'''God yield''' {{smaller|(or ’ild)}} '''you.''' {{smaller|See ''God''<sup>1</sup>, and def. 1 above.—}}'''To yield''' {{smaller|(or}} '''yield up) the breath.''' {{smaller|Same as ''to yield up the ghost.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O thou, whose wounds become hard-favour’d death,
